segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: After saying these things, Jesus went out with his disciples across the Kidron ravine, where there was a garden, which he and his disciples entered.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Now Judas, who was handing him over, also knew the place, because Jesus had often met there with his disciples.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So Judas took the cohort, along with officers from the chief priests and from the Pharisees, and came there with lanterns and torches and weapons.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Then Jesus, knowing everything that was coming upon him, went out and said to them,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Who are you looking for?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: They answered him,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Jesus of Nazareth.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He said to them,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “I am he.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And Judas, who was handing him over, was standing there with them.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So when he said to them,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “I am he,”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: they drew back and fell to the ground.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So he asked them again,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Who are you looking for?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And they said,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Jesus of Nazareth.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Jesus answered,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “I told you that I am he. So if it is me you are looking for, let these men go.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: This was to fulfill the word he had spoken:

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Of those you have given me, I have lost not one.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Then Simon Peter, who had a sword, drew it and struck the high priest’s slave and cut off his right ear. The slave’s name was Malchus.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So Jesus said to Peter,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Put the sword into its sheath. The cup the Father has given me—am I not to drink it?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So the cohort and its commander and the officers of the Jewish leaders arrested Jesus and bound him

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and led him first to Annas, for he was the father-in-law of Caiaphas, who was high priest that year.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Caiaphas was the one who had advised the Jewish leaders that it was better for one man to die for the people.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Simon Peter was following Jesus, and so was another disciple. That disciple was known to the high priest, and he went with Jesus into the high priest’s courtyard,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: but Peter stood outside at the door. So the other disciple, the one known to the high priest, went out and spoke to the woman who kept the door, and brought Peter in.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Then the slave girl who kept the door said to Peter,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “You are not one of this man’s disciples too, are you?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He said,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “I am not.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Now the slaves and the officers had made a charcoal fire, because it was cold, and they were standing there warming themselves. Peter too was with them, standing and warming himself.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Then the high priest questioned Jesus about his disciples and about his teaching.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Jesus answered him,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “I have spoken openly to the world. I always taught in synagogue and in the temple, where all the Jews come together, and I said nothing in secret.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: Why do you question me? Question those who heard what I said to them. Look, they know what I said.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: When he said this, one of the officers standing by gave Jesus a slap, saying,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Is that how you answer the high priest?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Jesus answered him,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “If I spoke wrongly, testify to what was wrong; but if rightly, why do you hit me?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Then Annas sent him, bound, to Caiaphas the high priest.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Meanwhile Simon Peter was standing and warming himself. So they said to him,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “You are not one of his disciples too, are you?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He denied it and said,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “I am not.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: One of the high priest’s slaves, a relative of the man whose ear Peter had cut off, said,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Did I not see you in the garden with him?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So Peter denied it again, and at once a rooster crowed.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Then they led Jesus from Caiaphas to the governor’s headquarters. It was early morning. They themselves did not enter the headquarters, so that they would not be defiled but could eat the Passover.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So Pilate came out to them and said,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “What accusation do you bring against this man?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: They answered him,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “If this man were not doing wrong, we would not have handed him over to you.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So Pilate said to them,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Take him yourselves and judge him according to your law.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The Jewish leaders said to him,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “We are not permitted to put anyone to death.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: This was to fulfill the word Jesus had spoken, indicating what kind of death he was going to die.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So Pilate went back into the headquarters, summoned Jesus, and said to him,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Are you the King of the Jews?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Jesus answered,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Are you saying this on your own, or did others tell you about me?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Pilate answered,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Am I a Jew? Your own nation and the chief priests handed you over to me. What have you done?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Jesus answered,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “My kingdom is not from this world. If my kingdom were from this world, my officers would be fighting so that I would not be handed over to the Jewish leaders. But as it is, my kingdom is not from here.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So Pilate said to him,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “So you are a king, then?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Jesus answered,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “You say that I am a king. For this I was born, and for this I have come into the world: to testify to the truth. Everyone who belongs to the truth listens to my voice.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Pilate said to him,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “What is truth?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Having said this, he went out again to the Jewish leaders and said to them,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “I find no grounds for a charge against him.

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: But you have a custom that I release someone to you at the Passover. So do you want me to release to you the King of the Jews?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So they shouted back,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Not this man, but Barabbas!”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Now Barabbas was a bandit.

notes.note: The Greek verb means ‘hand over’ or ‘deliver up’ and is the same one used in verses 30, 35 and 36 for the authorities handing Jesus over to Pilate. Most translations use ‘betray’ when Judas is the subject, and betrayal is certainly what the act amounts to, but the verb itself does not say so; Greek has a separate word for a traitor. Keeping one English verb lets the reader see the chain of handings-over that John traces through the chapter.

notes.traditional: a band of men; a detachment of soldiers
notes.note: This is the regular Greek term for a Roman cohort, a unit of auxiliary troops nominally about six hundred strong, though the word could also be used of a smaller detachment. John need not mean that the whole unit turned out. The ‘commander’ in verse 12 translates the Greek title used for a Roman military tribune, the officer in charge of a cohort. John thus presents Roman soldiers and the temple authorities’ own officers as acting together in the arrest.

The Greek is simply ‘I am’ (ego eimi). In ordinary speech this is how one says ‘That’s me’, and that is its surface meaning here. It is also the phrase with which God speaks in the Greek version of Isaiah, and which Jesus uses without a predicate earlier in John (8:58). The reaction in verse 6 suggests John intends the reader to hear both; some translations print ‘I AM’ to bring out the second sense.

The Greek word denotes a person owned by another, not a hired employee, and a first-century reader would have understood it so. ‘Servant’ is the older English rendering; several recent translations use ‘slave’. The ‘slave girl’ of verse 17 renders the corresponding feminine term.

The Greek says simply ‘the Jews’, the same word translated that way in verses 20, 33, 35 and 39. In John’s account of the arrest and trial the group in view is plainly the authorities in Jerusalem, not the Jewish people as a whole, and it is rendered accordingly here and in verses 14, 31, 36 and 38. Scholars are divided on the word generally: some argue for ‘Judeans’ throughout, while others object that this erases Jews from the New Testament.

John calls Caiaphas the high priest in verses 13 and 24, yet the questioner here appears to be Annas, since Jesus is sent on to Caiaphas only in verse 24. Annas had held the office from about AD 6 to 15 before being deposed by the Romans; he remained highly influential, and several members of his family held the office after him. Former high priests seem to have kept the title, which is the usual explanation of John’s wording.

notes.phrase: so that they would not be defiled
notes.note: Entering a Gentile’s residence was regarded as conveying ritual impurity, which would have barred a person from the Passover meal. In John’s account that meal still lies ahead on this morning, whereas in Matthew, Mark and Luke Jesus has already eaten the Passover with his disciples the evening before. The difference in chronology has long been discussed and is not settled.

notes.phrase: We are not permitted to put anyone to death
notes.traditional: It is not lawful for us to put any man to death
notes.note: In Roman provinces the power to execute was generally reserved to the governor. How strictly this applied in Judea is debated by historians, but John’s statement fits the general pattern. For John the point is the one made in verse 32: a Roman execution meant crucifixion, the ‘lifting up’ that Jesus had spoken of (12:32–33).
This is the same Greek word that in the plural is usually translated ‘Gentiles’ in this translation. Here, in the singular and in the mouth of a Roman, it means the Jewish people as a nation.

The Greek preposition states source or origin, as the closing words of the verse, ‘not from here’, confirm. The traditional ‘not of this world’ is easily heard as ‘otherworldly’ or ‘having nothing to do with this world’, which is not what the Greek says. The statement is about where Jesus’s kingship comes from and therefore how it operates, not about where it applies; some modern translations already use ‘from’.

The Greek word is the one used in verses 3, 12, 18 and 22 for the officers sent by the chief priests, and it means someone who carries out a superior’s orders. Most translations switch to ‘servants’ or ‘followers’ here. Keeping the same English word preserves John’s contrast between the officers who arrested Jesus and the officers Jesus says would be fighting for him if his kingdom were of that kind.

notes.phrase: You say that I am a king
notes.traditional: Thou sayest that I am a king
notes.note: The reply can be read as non-committal (‘king is your word’), as an affirmation (‘you are right to say that I am a king’), or, taking the Greek conjunction as ‘because’, as ‘You say so, because I am a king’. Most interpreters take it as a qualified acceptance: Jesus does not deny the title but goes on to define his purpose in terms of testifying to the truth. The rendering here leaves the reply as open as the Greek does.

The Greek word means an armed brigand who uses violence, not a thief. The Jewish historian Josephus uses it regularly for insurgents against Rome, and Mark and Luke connect Barabbas with an uprising and with murder. Some translations therefore render it ‘insurrectionist’ or paraphrase accordingly; ‘bandit’ keeps the word’s ordinary sense while allowing that overtone.

candidates.reason: Used of Judas, the authorities, Pilate and God across the Gospels and Paul; whether Judas ‘betrays’ or ‘hands over’ must be decided once or the verbal chain is lost.
Occurs throughout the New Testament and translators split between ‘slave’ and ‘servant’; no register entry was supplied for this chapter although the word occurs three times.
Recurs in the Gospels and Acts for temple officers, attendants and ministers of the word, with English varying between officer, guard, police, servant and attendant.
Used of Barabbas, the two crucified with Jesus, the ‘den’ in the temple saying and John 10; ‘robber’, ‘bandit’, ‘thief’ and ‘insurrectionist’ give readers quite different pictures.
The absolute use recurs in John (6:20; 8:24, 28, 58; 13:19; 18:5–8) and in Mark, and readers need a consistent policy on ‘I am he’, ‘It is I’ and ‘I am’.
